messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Andrew is a 37-year-old database administrator who came to therapy at the urging of his ex-wife, six months after their divorce was finalized. He had been living alone in a one-bedroom apartment near the office where he worked remotely, and his life had narrowed to a tight, predictable circuit: from his desk to his kitchen to his bed, and back again. What had begun as a frightening but survivable medical event three years earlier had, in Andrew’s experience, never truly ended.

The event itself had been a sudden pulmonary embolism. He had been sitting at his desk late one afternoon when a wave of breathlessness hit him without warning. He remembered the sensation of his chest tightening, the frantic shallow gasps that seemed to do nothing, and the growing certainty that he was going to suffocate right there in his ergonomic chair. A colleague called an ambulance, and Andrew spent the next five days in the intensive care unit, tethered to monitors and drips, watched over by a rotating cast of nurses whose faces he could no longer recall. What he remembered with perfect clarity was the moment a doctor inserted a central line into his neck—the cold antiseptic, the pressure, the needle sliding in as he lay frozen, unable to speak, convinced that this procedure was the last thing he would ever feel.

In the months that followed, Andrew was told he had made a full recovery. His follow-up scans were clear, his blood thinners were discontinued, and his pulmonologist discharged him with a handshake. But Andrew did not feel recovered. He had begun to notice, with a vigilance that felt entirely rational to him, that his body was no longer trustworthy. A slight tightness in his chest during a walk to the mailbox sent his heart racing. A stuffy room made him feel as though the air had been sucked out. He started to avoid exercise altogether, reasoning that if he never pushed his lungs, they would never fail him. He stopped going to the gym, stopped jogging, stopped climbing the stairs to his third-floor apartment and instead waited for the elevator even when it took five minutes to arrive.

His eating became rigid. He began to control his diet with a precision that felt like the only thing he could still manage. He ate the same small meals at the same times every day, terrified that any deviation—a heavy meal, a new food, a skipped snack—might trigger some internal imbalance that would bring back the breathlessness. He had come to believe that his body was a fragile machine, prone to catastrophic failure without his constant supervision.

The divorce had not been about the trauma, exactly, but the trauma had hollowed out the marriage. His wife had grown tired of planning social events around his need to know the location of every hospital in a ten-mile radius. She had stopped suggesting weekend trips because Andrew would spend the entire drive scanning the roadside for ambulances, flinching at the sight of a medical building. He had refused his annual physical for two years, and when she finally pressured him to go, he had walked out of the waiting room before the nurse could call his name. The sight of the examination table, the gleam of the blood pressure cuff, the faint antiseptic smell—it all hit him like a wave of suffocation, and he had fled. She had called him unreasonable. He had called her unsympathetic. Neither was wrong.

Now, in the present, Andrew’s world had become almost unbearably small. He worked from home and ordered groceries delivered so he would never have to pass the pharmacy or the urgent care clinic on the way to the supermarket. He had not seen a doctor in three years. His body felt constantly tense, as though bracing for a blow that never landed. At night, he often woke with his heart pounding, gasping for air that was perfectly available, and he would lie in the dark, certain that this was the moment it would happen again. What frightened him most was the feeling itself—the terror that flooded him when he noticed his own breathing, the way his body seemed to betray him with every skipped heartbeat or shallow inhale. He had come to believe that the fear itself was a sign that something was wrong, that his own panic was proof that he was not safe.

He finally called for an appointment after a minor cold left him housebound for a week, too afraid to sleep, too afraid to rest, hypervigilant to every rattle in his chest. He told the intake coordinator that he wanted to stop being afraid of his own body. What he did not say, but what he hoped with a quiet desperation, was that someone might finally show him how to breathe without fearing that each breath would be his last.
